Audi Q9 Debuts World's First Curved Digital OLED, Panel Thin as a Human Hair
18 photos
Photo: Audi
Not that long ago, car lights moved from being used to make the road ahead visible during the night to becoming a symbol of status and, in certain circumstances, communication tools with the exterior world. They are, if you will, smart lights, and they appear to become even smarter as time goes by.
Audi is one of the carmakers that has always been at the forefront of R&D in the field of vehicle lights, having implemented, for instance, OLED technology on the Audi TT RS about a decade ago. It has continuously tried to make that tech better, and here's the latest version of Audi's car lights, coming in a form never seen before in the industry.
Before getting into it, a quick reminder of what OLED (organic light-emitting diode) is: a semiconductor light source that uses stacked layers of organic molecules to recombine electrons in various ways once a voltage is applied.
In the version announced this week, Audi's digital OLED technology hides all that underneath one of the thinnest glass surfaces around. That would be only 0.1 millimeters thick, which is about the same as the thickness of a human hair.
Using such panels allowed Audi to bend the assembly on a radius of up to 200 millimeters, closely following the contours of whatever car it is fitted on. In this case, that would be the new Q9.
Audi calls the launch of this hardware on the big SUV a technological world first. For the driver, other drivers, and perhaps even pedestrians, the solution not only makes the Q9 visible from the back and from the sides, but can also be used to communicate things depending on what the OLED shows using semi-active digital light signatures with 3D effects.
As used on this vehicle, the OLED consists of 512 segments placed on six panels. Among them, the curved outer panel made of 99 segments, the middle one with 84 segments, and an inner panel with 73 segments. All of this makes this one the largest OLED panel Audi has ever produced so far.
The tech supports up to eight digital light signatures, which can be shown, for the first time, in a semi-active fashion, making them particularly striking, especially in the dead of night.
Audi did not say when the tech will expand to cover other models in its lineup, but we'll keep an eye on things and report back once we know more about that.
As for the Q9 that's involved in this evolution of rear lights, the luxury SUV starts on the American market at $118,000 for the SQ9 version. It's unclear at the time of writing whether the curved OLED lights will be included as standard or offered as optional extras.
